channel.title: SnapDisk blog
channel.description: How to back up photos to a USB drive on Android — no cloud, no account, no upload.

item.title: How to back up photos to a USB drive without uploading them
item.description: Your photos don't need a cloud to be safe. A USB drive plugged into your phone holds the whole backup — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

item.title: USB photo backup on Android: back up photos to an external drive without uploading them
item.description: Your phone's camera roll fits on a drive you can hold. A USB photo backup keeps the whole copy in your pocket — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

item.title: How to back up DCIM to OTG storage on Android
item.description: DCIM is where your Android phone keeps its camera photos — and OTG is how a USB drive plugs straight into that phone. Put the two together and your whole camera roll copies to a drive you can hold, with no computer and no upload in between.

item.title: How to copy photos to a USB stick on Android
item.description: A USB stick is the simplest photo backup there is: no account, no upload, no monthly fee — just your photos on a drive you can hold. And on Android you don't need a computer in between: the stick plugs straight into the phone.

item.title: How to back up photos offline on Android — no cloud, no account
item.description: Most "backup" apps start by uploading your photos to someone else's server. An offline backup never does: your photos copy from your phone straight to a drive you can hold, with no account, no upload, and nothing to log into.

item.title: How to back up photos to an external drive on Android
item.description: An external drive is the simplest photo backup there is: a drive you can hold, with your photos on it, and no cloud in between. On Android the drive plugs straight into the phone — no computer needed.

item.title: How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive
item.description: Your phone is full because your photos are. Move them to a USB drive you can hold, check the copy, then delete the originals — and the storage warning goes away without losing a single picture.

item.title: SnapDisk vs VaultDrive: USB photo backup on Android, compared
item.description: Two Android apps that copy your photos to a USB drive — no cloud, no account, no upload. Here is how they actually differ, from the facts we could verify as of November 2026.

item.title: Back up WhatsApp photos to a USB drive on Android (no computer)
item.description: Your WhatsApp photos are files on your phone — in a folder you can point a backup app at. Plug a USB drive into the phone and copy them straight to it, no computer, no upload.

item.title: Transfer photos from Android to a USB drive automatically (no manual copy)
item.description: Moving photos to a USB drive by hand means opening a file manager, picking files one by one, and hoping nothing gets missed. Plug the drive in, tap once, and let the whole library copy itself.

item.title: Back up Samsung Galaxy photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Galaxy phones are the most common Android phones there are, and Samsung gives you two ways to get photos onto a USB drive — but neither one is a photo backup that runs itself. Here is what Samsung offers, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Google Pixel photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Pixel phones have no SD-card slot and no Samsung-style file manager — but a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up OnePlus photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: OnePlus phones hide one extra switch before a USB drive works at all — OxygenOS turns OTG off unless you enable it. Once it's on, a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is My Files. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Xiaomi photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Xiaomi phones hide one extra switch before a USB drive works at all — on many MIUI and HyperOS phones OTG is off unless you enable it, and it switches itself off after about 10 minutes. Once it's on, a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Mi File Manager. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Motorola photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Motorola phones run near-stock Android, so there is no OTG switch to hunt for — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up videos from Android to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Videos are the files that fill a phone first — and the ones the manual copy handles worst, one long file at a time. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Huawei photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Huawei phones have their own built-in backup app, but it writes an encrypted archive — not plain photos you can open anywhere. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is the Files app. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Sony Xperia photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Sony's Xperia phones run near-stock Android with almost no Sony apps on board — Google Photos is the gallery, Files by Google is the file manager — and Sony's own backup tool needs a PC. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up LG photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: LG stopped making phones in 2021, so no LG guide or LG tool will ever be written for this — and LG's own backup tools move data phone-to-phone or phone-to-PC, never phone-to-USB as plain photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Oppo photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Oppo's ColorOS hides one switch between you and a USB drive — OTG Connection, which turns itself off after about 10 minutes unused — and Oppo's own backup tools move photos to another phone or to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Realme photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Realme's Realme UI hides one switch between you and a USB drive — OTG Connection, which turns itself off after about 10 minutes unused — and Realme's own backup tools move photos to another phone or to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Vivo photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Vivo's Funtouch OS hides one switch between you and a USB drive — OTG, under Settings > More settings, which turns itself off if it is not used in 5 minutes — and Vivo's own backup tools move photos to another phone, to a PC, or to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Honor photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Honor's MagicOS has no documented OTG switch to hunt for — the drive mounts on plug-in on most models, with a "USB storage added" notification — and Honor's own backup tools write an encrypted backup package, move photos to another phone or a PC, or back them up to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Nokia photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Nokia phones (made by HMD Global) run near-stock Android — Android One on most models — with no OTG switch to hunt for: the drive mounts on plug-in on most models, with a "USB storage added" notification. And Nokia has no backup app of its own: HMD's own guides point to Google backup, which restores to a new phone or to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Asus photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Asus phones (Zenfone and ROG Phone) run ZenUI — close to stock Android on recent models — with no OTG switch to hunt for: the drive mounts on plug-in on most models, with a "USB storage added" notification. And Asus's own backup tool moves your data to a new Asus phone, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Infinix photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Infinix phones (Note, Hot, Zero, and GT series) run XOS — Infinix's Android skin — with OTG support that varies by model: most recent models mount the drive on plug-in with a “USB storage added” notification, but some budget models have no OTG at all. And Infinix's own backup tools back your photos up to the cloud or to a PC, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Tecno photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Tecno phones (Spark, Camon, Pova, Phantom, and Pop series) run HiOS — Tecno's Android skin — with OTG support that varies by model: most recent models mount the drive on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification, but support is not universal, and some older models list OTG in the specs without it working out of the box. And Tecno's own backup tools back your photos up to the cloud, to an SD card, or to a PC, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Tecno. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Nothing Phone photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Nothing phones (Phone (1), Phone (2), Phone (2a), and the CMF Phone 1) run Nothing OS — a near-stock Android skin — with OTG support on the main Phone models: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Phone (1), Phone (2), Phone (2a), and Phone (2a) Plus, and Nothing's own support site documents OTG as a feature — but the CMF Phone 1 is the exception to check, because spec tables disagree on whether it supports OTG at all. And Nothing's own backup tools are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any Nothing phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up POCO photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: POCO phones (F, X, and M series) run HyperOS — Xiaomi's Android skin, since POCO is Xiaomi's sub-brand — with OTG support on the F and X series: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the F7, F7 Pro, X7, and X7 Pro, and USB Type-C 3.2 with OTG for the F9 Ultra — but the budget M series is the exception to check, because spec tables disagree on whether the M7 supports OTG at all. And POCO's own backup tools are Xiaomi Cloud and Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any POCO phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Redmi photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Redmi phones (Note, K, and A series) run HyperOS — Xiaomi's Android skin, since Redmi is Xiaomi's sub-brand — with OTG support across the Note 14 line: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Note 14 Pro 4G and the Note 14 Pro 5G — but the microSD slot varies by model: the Note 14 Pro 4G has a microSDXC slot (uses the shared SIM slot) while the Note 14 Pro 5G has none. And Redmi's own backup tools are Xiaomi Cloud and Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any Redmi phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up iQOO photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: iQOO phones (13, 12, Neo, and Z series) run Funtouch OS outside China — OriginOS on the China models — since iQOO is Vivo's sub-brand, with OTG across the current lines: spec tables list USB Type-C 3.2 with OTG for the iQOO 13 and USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the iQOO 12, the Neo 10, and the Z10 Turbo Pro. And iQOO's own backup tools are iQOO Cloud (vivo Cloud) and Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools, which back your photos up to the cloud or to a computer, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current iQOO phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up TCL photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: TCL phones (50, 40, and 30 series) run TCL UI — TCL's Android skin — with OTG across the current lines: spec tables list USB Type-C with OTG for the 50 XL NxtPaper and the 50 XE NxtPaper. And TCL has no backup tool of its own: the routes on a TCL phone are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools, which back your photos up to the cloud or to a computer, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current TCL phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up ZTE photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: ZTE phones (Axon, Blade, and nubia/RedMagic) run MyOS — ZTE's Android skin — with OTG on some models but not others: spec tables list USB Type-C with OTG for the Axon 60 and the Axon 60 Ultra, while the Blade V30, the Blade V8, and the Axon 40 Lite have no OTG at all. And ZTE has no backup tool of its own: the routes on a ZTE phone are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools, which back your photos up to the cloud or to a computer, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a current Axon phone that supports OTG. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Fairphone photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Fairphone phones (4, 5, and 6) run Fairphone OS — near-stock Android — with USB-C and OTG on all three: spec tables list USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG and DisplayPort for the Fairphone 4 and the Fairphone 5, and USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Fairphone 6. And Fairphone has no backup tool of its own: the routes on a Fairphone are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools and rooted backup apps, which back your photos up to the cloud, to a computer, or to another device, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Fairphone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Sharp Aquos photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Sharp Aquos phones (R10, R9, and sense9) run near-stock Android with USB-C and OTG on all three: spec tables list USB Type-C 3.2 with OTG for the Aquos R10 and the Aquos sense9, and USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Aquos R9. And Sharp has no backup tool of its own: the routes on a Sharp Aquos are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus, on Japan carrier models, docomo Data Copy to a microSD card, which back your photos up to the cloud, to a card, or to another phone, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Aquos. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Lenovo photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Lenovo phones (K13, K13 Pro, and the Legion gaming phones) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the K13, USB-C with OTG for the K13 Pro, and two USB-C ports with OTG for the Legion Phone Duel and the Legion 2 Pro — and even the budget K12 has OTG over micro-USB. And Lenovo has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its own tool is Software Fix (formerly Rescue and Smart Assistant), a Windows PC app that backs your pictures up to a PC before a rescue, and the other routes are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any USB-C Lenovo. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up HTC photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: HTC phones (U23 Pro, Desire 22 Pro, and U23) have USB-C and OTG across the current range: spec tables list USB-C 3.0 with OTG for the U23 Pro, USB-C 2.0 with OTG for the Desire 22 Pro, and USB-C 3.0 with OTG for the U23 — and HTC's own support pages for the U12+ and the U12 life describe viewing files from a USB drive over OTG. And HTC has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its own tool is HTC Sync Manager, a desktop app that backs your pictures up to a PC — and it is discontinued, support ended — and the other routes are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current HTC. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Blackview photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Blackview rugged phones (BV9300, BV9300 Pro, and BV6200 Pro) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C with OTG for the BV9300, OTG reverse charging for the BV9300 Pro, and OTG for the BV6200 Pro — and Blackview's own backup guide lists USB OTG as an external-storage option you can copy files to by hand. And Blackview has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its own guide's six ways are a Google account backup, a local backup to a computer, third-party backup apps, a manual copy to external storage, ADB, and custom recovery — none of them an automated phone-to-USB copy. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Blackview. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Ulefone photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Ulefone Armor phones (Armor 28 Ultra, Armor 34 Pro, Armor 27 Pro, and Armor Mini 20) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list OTG support for the Armor 28 Ultra and the Armor 34 Pro, USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Armor 27 Pro, and USB OTG expansion for the Armor Mini 20 — and Ulefone has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with TWRP and Titanium Backup for experts. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Ulefone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Doogee photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Doogee rugged phones (S118 Pro, S118, and S98) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the S118 Pro, the S118 Pro manual lists OTG with reverse charging, and the S98 lists On-The-Go among its USB features — and Doogee has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with a microSD card as the local option. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Doogee. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up CAT photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: CAT rugged phones (S75, S62 Pro, and S53) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the S75 and the S62 Pro, and USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG for the S53 — and CAT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with a microSD card as the local option. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current CAT. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Oukitel photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Oukitel rugged phones (WP39, WP35, and WP33 Pro) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the WP39 and the WP35, and the WP33 Pro manual lists 18W reverse charging over OTG — and Oukitel has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with a microSD card as the local option. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Oukitel. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up AGM photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: AGM rugged phones (H6, H6 Pro, and H6 Lite) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the H6 and the H6 Pro, and USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go for the H6 Lite, and AGM's own product page lists OTG among the H6's features — and AGM has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the H6 manual's storage mention is Drive, Google's cloud, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current AGM. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Cubot photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Cubot rugged phones (KingKong X, KingKong 11, and KingKong Mini 4) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the KingKong X, the KingKong 11, and the KingKong Mini 4, and the KingKong Dura lists USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG too — and Cubot has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google cloud, or root-only tools, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Cubot. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Unihertz photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Unihertz phones (Titan 2, Titan Pocket, Jelly 2, Jelly Star, and Tank) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the Tank, USB on-the-go for the Titan Pocket and the Tank 2, USB OTG for the Titan 2, and USB OTG for the Jelly 2 and the Jelly Star — and Unihertz has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model FAQ pages all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Unihertz. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Hotwav photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Hotwav phones (Cyber 13 Pro, Note 13 Pro, and Note 13 Max) have USB-C and OTG across the range: the Note 13 Pro spec table lists OTG as Yes, and the Note 13 Max, the Note 13 Pro, and the Cyber 13 Pro all ship an OTG cable in the box — and Hotwav has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the user manuals' backup advice is only to regularly back up your data to cloud storage or an external device, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Hotwav. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up IIIF150 photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: IIIF150 phones (B3C, Air3, and B2 Ultra) have USB-C and OTG across the range: the B3C spec table lists OTG as Support, the Air3 and the B2 Ultra list USB On-The-Go as Yes, and the Air1 Ultra and the Air2 Ultra list it too — and IIIF150 has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model FAQ pages point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current IIIF150. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up RugGear photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: RugGear's Android phones (RG655, RG850, and RG880) have USB host support on at least the RG655 — the RG655 spec table lists USB OTG as Yes, the RG310 lists USB on-the-go, and the RG935 tablet lists OTG as supported — and RugGear has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the RG655 manual gives no backup advice at all, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. One honest caveat up front: the RG850 and RG880 datasheets I found do not list OTG either way, so check with a drive before relying on it, and the RG655 has a micro USB port, so it needs a micro-USB OTG adapter while the RG850 and RG880 are USB-C. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Sonim photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Sonim's Android phones (XP8 and XP10) have USB host support on at least the XP8 — the XP8 user guide lists the USB-C port as "High Speed, OTG" — and Sonim has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: Sonim SCOUT is a device-management app, not a backup, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. One honest caveat up front: the XP10 datasheet I found does not list OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it, and the XP5s is not an Android phone at all — it runs a proprietary OS, so SnapDisk cannot install on it. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Kyocera photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Kyocera's DuraForce Android phones (Pro 2, Ultra 5G, PRO 3, and DuraSport) have USB host support on at least two of them — the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the DuraForce Pro 2, and the DuraSport's spec pages list its port as "USB Type-C, USB On-The-Go" — and Kyocera has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Ultra 5G and PRO 3 datasheets list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it on those models, and the older DuraForce phones are out of scope — the original DuraForce runs Android 4.4, the DuraForce XD runs Android 5.1, and the original DuraForce PRO's spec tables list USB OTG as No. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Crosscall photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Crosscall's rugged Android phones (Core-X5, Action-X5, Core-Z5, and Stellar-X5) have USB host support on at least three of them — the spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes for the Core-X5, Crosscall's own product sheet lists OTG as Yes for the Action-X5, and the Core-Z5 spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes — and Crosscall has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Stellar-X5 spec pages I found list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it on that model, and the older Trekker-M1 phones are out of scope — they run Android 5.1, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Hammer photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Hammer's rugged Android phones (Blade V 5G, Iron 4, Blade 3, and Explorer Pro) have USB-C ports, and the only per-model OTG listings I found are FindPare's — USB OTG as Yes for the Energy 18x9 and the Blade 2 Pro — but FindPare itself says its information is not ascertained, and the current models' spec pages list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it — and Hammer has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Hammer 6 LTE is a feature phone, not an Android phone at all, so SnapDisk cannot install on it, and the original Hammer Iron runs Android 4.2 and the AXE M LTE runs Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up FOSSiBOT photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: FOSSiBOT's rugged F-series Android phones (F101, F101 Pro, F102, F107 Pro, F110 Pro 5G, F112 Pro, and F113) list USB OTG support in their spec tables, and FOSSiBOT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. Two honest caveats up front: the F101P's official page mentions OTG only as reverse charging — powering another device from the phone's battery, not hosting a drive — and the F115 Ultra's spec data conflicts (one source lists USB OTG as false while also listing USB-C as false), so check Settings > Storage on those two models before relying on it; and the original F101 went on sale in October 2020, and I did not verify its Android version in the sources above, so owners of that model should check Settings > About phone — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up UMIDIGI Bison photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: UMIDIGI's rugged Bison line (Bison, Bison Pro, Bison Plus, Bison 2 Pro, Bison X10, Bison X10G, and Bison X10 Pro) lists USB OTG support in its spec tables, and UMIDIGI has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. Three honest caveats up front: the Bison X20's OTG host support is unverified — one source lists OTG Support as No, the others list USB Type-C only, and the reviews mention OTG reverse charging only — and the Bison GT, the Bison GT2 Pro, the Bison GT2 Pro 5G, the Bison X10S, and the Bison X10S NFC have no OTG listing in the sources I found, so check Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it; the original Bison's connector itself is disputed between sources — GSMArena and MySmartPrice list USB-C, while mobility.com.ng lists microUSB — so check your own port before buying an adapter; and I did not verify the Android version of the Bison X10, X10G, or X10 Pro in the sources above, so owners of those models should check Settings > About phone — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Energizer photos to a USB drive (no computer)
